title: LEVITICUS 20 GIVES A SERIOUS PENALTY FOR SEX DURING MENSTRUATION—BUT DOES THIS LAW STILL APPLY TO CHRISTIANS?
paragraphs: LEVITICUS 20 GIVES A SERIOUS PENALTY FOR SEX DURING MENSTRUATION—BUT DOES THIS LAW STILL APPLY TO CHRISTIANS?

One disturbing verse. One severe consequence. And one question many Christians are almost afraid to ask: If we believe the whole Bible is the Word of God, what are we supposed to do with Leviticus 20:18?
There are verses in the Bible people underline.
There are verses people frame on walls.
There are verses Christians memorize when life is falling apart.
And then there are verses we quietly pass over because we are not quite sure what to do with them.
Leviticus 20:18 is one of those verses.
Read slowly what the King James Version says:

“And if a man shall lie with a woman having her sickness, and shall uncover her nakedness; he hath discovered her fountain, and she hath uncovered the fountain of her blood: and both of them shall be cut off from among their people.”
—Leviticus 20:18, KJV
That is not a comfortable verse.
And perhaps it should not be.
But discomfort is not permission to distort Scripture.
Some people will read this and immediately conclude, “See? The Old Testament is cruel.”
Others will respond from the opposite direction and say, “God said it, so Christians must still enforce it exactly as ancient Israel did.”
Both reactions can move too quickly.
Because before asking, “Do Christians have to obey this?” we need to ask a more fundamental question:
What exactly did God command, to whom did He give the command, what did the command mean within the covenant God made with Israel, and what changed when Jesus Christ established the New Covenant?
That journey takes us somewhere much deeper than menstruation.
It takes us into holiness.
Covenant.
Sin.
Blood.
Grace.
And ultimately...
Jesus.
The Hebrew text of Leviticus 20:18 begins:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִשְׁכַּב אֶת־אִשָּׁה דָּוָה
Ve’ish asher-yishkav et-ishah davah...
In straightforward terms:
“And a man who lies with a menstruating woman...”

The word דָּוָה (davah) describes the woman in connection with her menstrual condition. The verse then says that the man has “uncovered her nakedness” and exposed her מָקוֹר (maqor)—her source or fountain—and that she has uncovered the source of her blood.
Then comes the frightening conclusion:
וְנִכְרְתוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם מִקֶּרֶב עַמָּם
Venikhretu sheneihem miqqerev ‘ammam.
“And both of them shall be cut off from among their people.”
Notice something immediately.
The Hebrew does not say, “Both of them shall be stoned.”
It does not explicitly say, “Execute them.”
It says they are to be “cut off”—from the Hebrew root כרת (karat).
That distinction matters.

The expression translated “cut off” appears elsewhere in the Torah and has generated considerable discussion concerning precisely how the sanction was understood—whether exclusion from the covenant community, divine judgment, premature death, loss of descendants, or some combination depending on context.
So we should not make Leviticus 20:18 say more than it actually says.
But neither should we make it say less.
This was serious.
Very serious.
Within Israel’s covenant life, this was not presented as an insignificant private matter.
And this is where the question becomes uncomfortable for modern Christians.
Why?
Why would God care about something so intimate?
To understand that, you have to walk backward several chapters.

Leviticus 15 discusses bodily discharges and ritual uncleanness. Menstruation made a woman ceremonially unclean for a period of time. Contact with certain things associated with that condition could communicate ritual uncleanness.
That did not mean the woman was morally disgusting.
It did not mean menstruation itself was a personal sin.
That distinction is absolutely essential.
Biblical ritual uncleanness and personal moral guilt are not identical categories.

People could become ceremonially unclean through ordinary realities of embodied human life. The book of Leviticus carefully regulates how Israel approached the holy presence of God, and categories of clean and unclean formed part of that covenant system.
In fact, Leviticus 15:24 says that if a man lies with a menstruating woman and her menstrual impurity comes upon him, he becomes unclean for seven days.
Then Leviticus 18:19 goes further and explicitly commands:
“Also thou shalt not approach unto a woman to uncover her nakedness, as long as she is put apart for her uncleanness.”
Then Leviticus 20:18 gives the corresponding sanction.
So we should not flatten these passages into one sentence.
Leviticus 15 discusses ritual impurity.
Leviticus 18 gives a prohibition.
Leviticus 20 attaches a serious covenant consequence.
The Bible is doing more than saying, “Blood is gross.”
That modern caricature completely misses the theological world of Leviticus.
Blood had enormous significance in Israel’s worship.
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood...”
—Leviticus 17:11
Blood represented life.
Blood belonged profoundly within Israel’s sacrificial symbolism.
Blood was associated with purification, sacrifice, atonement, life, death, and approach to a holy God.
And Leviticus repeatedly teaches Israel something modern humanity desperately wants to forget:
God is holy.
Not casually holy.
Not symbolically holy.
Not holy only when holiness happens to agree with our preferences.
Holy.
The Hebrew word is קָדוֹשׁ—qadosh.
Set apart.
Distinct.
God was teaching Israel that approaching Him was not casual business.
Their bodies mattered.
Their sexuality mattered.
Their worship mattered.
Their relationships mattered.
Their blood mattered.
Their obedience mattered.
Their covenant mattered.
This is where many readers make a mistake.
We open Leviticus as twenty-first-century Christians and instinctively ask, “Which of these rules do I personally have to follow?”
But Leviticus was originally given within the Mosaic covenant to Israel.
It was not dropped out of heaven as an isolated collection of random regulations addressed identically to every nation in every historical covenant setting.
Israel was a covenant people.
God had redeemed them from Egypt.
He had bound Himself to them.
He gave them priesthood, sacrifices, purity regulations, civil judgments, festivals, dietary distinctions, circumcision, tabernacle worship, and laws governing life in the covenant community.
And then Jesus came.
This is where the story turns.
Not because the Old Testament was a mistake.
Not because holiness stopped mattering.
Not because God suddenly changed His personality.
Jesus came because everything toward which the Law was moving finds its ultimate fulfillment in Him.
At the Last Supper, Jesus took the cup and declared:
“This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.”
—Luke 22:20, KJV
There it is again.
Blood.
But now...
His blood.
The book of Hebrews explains the enormous covenantal significance of what Christ accomplished.
“In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old.”
—Hebrews 8:13, KJV
Christians therefore do not live under the Mosaic covenant as ancient Israel lived under it.
That does not mean Christians tear Leviticus out of the Bible.
It means we read Leviticus through the fulfillment brought by Jesus Christ.
This distinction is visible almost immediately in the early Church.
When Gentiles began coming to Christ, the apostles faced an enormous question.
Would Gentile believers have to enter the Mosaic covenant and bear its requirements in the same manner as Jewish Israel?
Acts 15 records the Jerusalem Council wrestling with that very issue.
The apostles did not command Gentile converts to become Israel under the Mosaic covenant.
Yet—and this matters enormously—they did not conclude that grace means moral chaos.
They specifically instructed believers to abstain from idolatry, blood, things strangled, and sexual immorality (Acts 15:28–29).
Grace did not erase holiness.
Grace changed our covenant relationship to the Law.
That is why the Christian response to Leviticus 20:18 cannot simply be:
“That is Old Testament. Ignore it.”
No.
Christians should never be embarrassed by something God chose to reveal.
We should study it.
Understand its covenant setting.
Ask what it reveals about God's holiness.
Recognize how the New Testament treats the Mosaic covenant.
And then bring the entire matter to Christ.
So does Leviticus 20:18 mean Christians today should “cut off” a husband and wife who have sexual intercourse during menstruation?
Christians are not authorized by the New Testament to recreate ancient Israel’s covenant sanctions and impose Leviticus 20:18 as a civil or ecclesiastical penalty.
The Church is not ancient Israel's theocratic civil government.
Jesus established the New Covenant.
The apostolic Church did not simply transfer every Mosaic purity regulation and its associated national sanctions into Christian church discipline.
But that answer should not become an excuse for another dangerous error:
“Then Leviticus has nothing to teach us.”
It has everything to teach us about the God we worship.
It reminds us that God has never treated sexuality as spiritually meaningless.
Our culture often says that what consenting adults do sexually is nobody else's concern.
Scripture never gives sexuality that kind of spiritual independence.
Your body belongs to God.
Your marriage belongs to God.
Your desires belong under the lordship of Christ.
Your sexuality is not a tiny kingdom where Jesus has no throne.
Paul would later write:
—1 Corinthians 6:19–20, KJV
Read those words again.
“You are not your own.”
That sentence collides violently with modern individualism.
We want Jesus as Savior while keeping certain rooms locked.
My money.
My body.
My sexuality.
My relationship.
My entertainment.
My secret habits.
My private messages.
My browser history.
My resentment.
My addiction.
My hidden fantasy.
My life.
And Jesus stands at the door of every room we have labeled “private.”
Not because He wants to destroy us.
Because He purchased us.
The Christian life is not Jesus decorating the parts of your old life you are willing to show Him.
It is death and resurrection.
It is surrender.
And maybe that is why a strange verse in Leviticus can suddenly become painfully personal.
Because perhaps your issue has nothing to do with Leviticus 20:18.
Perhaps your issue is the room you refuse to surrender.
The relationship you know is pulling you from Christ.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The bitterness you have baptized as “boundaries.”
The affair hidden behind deleted messages.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The secret compromise you keep promising God you will abandon “soon.”
The Sunday worship followed by Monday surrender to the same chains.
You came here wondering about menstrual sex.
And somehow Scripture turned the mirror toward you.
That is what the Word of God does.
“For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword...”
—Hebrews 4:12, KJV
It cuts through our performances.
Through religious vocabulary.
Through excuses.
Through carefully edited Christian appearances.
And eventually it reaches the place where we cannot hide.
But please hear what happens next.
Because Christianity does not end with exposure.
If exposure were the end, every one of us would be finished.
The same Bible that reveals God's holiness reveals something even more astonishing.
A holy God came looking for unholy people.
Not with lowered standards.
With pierced hands.
Jesus did not come to announce that sin had stopped mattering.
He came because sin mattered so much that redemption would cost blood.
His blood.
The ancient sacrificial system had trained generations of Israelites to understand that approaching holiness was costly.
Then outside Jerusalem, the Lamb of God was nailed to wood.
Blood ran from His wounds.
The innocent for the guilty.
The righteous for the unrighteous.
The Holy One for sinners.
And suddenly the Bible's long story of holiness, sacrifice, blood, cleansing, covenant, priesthood, and forgiveness converged on a crucified Messiah.
Jesus was not Plan B.
He was the Lamb “foreordained before the foundation of the world” (1 Peter 1:20).
At the cross, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
He dealt with it.
And when Jesus rose from the dead, grace walked out of the tomb alive.
That is why there is hope for the sexually broken.
Hope for the adulterer.
Hope for the porn addict.
Hope for the ashamed.
Hope for the religious hypocrite.
Hope for the person who knew better and did it anyway.
Hope for the person carrying memories they wish they could erase.
Hope for the person reading this quietly thinking:
“If everyone knew what I had done, they would never look at me the same.”
Jesus already knows.
Every chapter.
Every deleted scene.
Every secret.
Every night.
Every compromise.
Every wound.
Every sin.
And the Gospel is not the announcement that those things do not matter.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ is greater.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
Cleanse.
There is a word Leviticus prepares us to understand.
We spend enormous energy trying to look clean.
Jesus came to make sinners clean.
Not through ritual performance.
Not through pretending.
Not through social-media Christianity.
Through His blood.
Through repentance.
Through faith.
Through grace.
Through a Savior who died and rose again.
Maybe you have spent years hiding.
Maybe people call you strong.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
Maybe you can quote Scripture while carrying a private war nobody sees.
Then stop performing for one moment.
God already knows.
You do not have to impress the One who watched you fall.
You need to surrender to the One who can raise you.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the door through which you stop running from the only One who can actually save you.
Turn to Jesus.
Confess what needs confessing.
Leave what needs leaving.
Repair what can be repaired.
Seek help where help is needed.
Bring darkness into light.
Not because obedience purchases salvation.
Because the Savior who purchased you is worthy of your obedience.
And if you stumbled onto this article because somebody shared it...
Maybe they were not judging you.
Maybe they were thinking about you because they love you.
Maybe this is the conversation you have avoided.
Maybe God is using an uncomfortable verse from Leviticus to remind you that He still wants every part of your life.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to write the details publicly.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become another person's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Neither honors the whole biblical story.
We need the Law.
We need the prophets.
We need the apostles.
And above all, we need Jesus Christ—the One toward whom the Scriptures lead.
That share matters more than you may realize.
Someone may be drifting from Christianity because nobody ever helped them understand the Bible in context.
Someone may be drowning in secret shame.
Someone may be convinced that what they have done has permanently disqualified them from grace.
Let this reach them.
At the cross, they meet.
Help us keep going.
Christian ministry requires people willing not only to receive but also to participate—to pray, share, serve, give, and help truth travel farther than it could travel without them.
Your giving before God is a matter of faithful Christian stewardship, conscience, and conviction.
Supporting Gospel work can glorify God when it flows from love for Christ rather than pressure, appearance, or manipulation.
Paul described Christian generosity this way:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
From the heart.
That is the kind of support we want.
But the deeper reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the person who is angry with God.
Invite the seeker with questions Christians sometimes seem afraid to answer.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing intelligent to say.
And keep sharing.
Because sometimes evangelism begins with a pulpit.
Sometimes it begins across a kitchen table.
And sometimes it begins when one Christian presses “Share” and a wounded person, alone at 1:37 in the morning, finds exactly the truth they were about to stop searching for.
Leviticus 20:18 is serious.
We should let it be serious.
It belonged to the covenant God made with Israel, and Christians should neither rip it from that covenant setting nor pretend it never existed.
It reminds us that the God of Scripture is holy.
It reminds us that sexuality belongs under His authority.
It reminds us that blood, purity, covenant, and access to God's presence run deeply through the biblical story.
But Leviticus is not the end of that story.
There is another covenant.
Another Priest.
Another sacrifice.
Another blood.
Jesus Christ entered the story.
And for the sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith, the final word is no longer simply:
Unclean.
Outcast.
Condemned.
The Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful.
Forgiven.
Cleansed.
Redeemed.
Adopted.
Made new.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear more than the answer to the original question.
God's holiness is more terrifying than modern Christianity sometimes admits.
Your sin is more serious than your excuses have allowed you to believe.
But the blood of Jesus is more powerful than the darkest chapter you have ever written.
So stop hiding.
Come home.
And remember this when shame tries to introduce you by your worst moment:
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story—but when Jesus takes the pen, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
